entries.title: Step 0 · The plan, and five rules that prevent predictable failures
entries.summary: Every Python project follows the same spine: folder → environment → Git → package scaffold → data → code with tests → run and log → ship. This tab walks it once, building a small character-level GPT from an empty folder, so you can copy the sequence for your own project. Each step shows the exact commands, what every line does, and the real output.
entries.example:
Part I    Set up    1 folder · 2 conda env · 3 check · 4 git init
                    5 GitHub repo · 6 connect · 7 scaffold
Part II   Data      8 download script · 9 clean · 10 tokenizer · 11 split & batch
Part III  Models    12 baseline · 13 config · 14 transformer
Part IV   Run       15 smoke run · 16 full run · 17 evaluate · 18 test suite
Part V    Ship      19 Colab · 20 branches · 21 pull request · 22 README
lines: Environment before Git

Create the conda environment and install the packages first, so the very first commit already records what the code needs to run. A repository whose first commit cannot be installed is one nobody can reproduce.
.gitignore before the first commit
Commit a 1 MB data file once and it lives in the history forever. Ignore rules go in before anything is staged.
A walking skeleton before the real model
Get a tiny model running end to end in seconds, then scale up. Otherwise your first debugging session and your first long training run happen at the same time, and you will not know which is broken.
A baseline before the neural network
Thirty lines of counting give you a number to beat. Without it, “my loss is 2.1” means nothing; with it you know 2.1 is worse than counting letter pairs.
Tests alongside, not at the end
Every module gets its test in the same sitting. Unit tests (does the code do what I said) and evaluation (is the model any good) are different jobs and live in different folders.
entries.gotcha: The order matters more than the tools. With venv instead of conda, or pytest instead of unittest, the spine is exactly the same.
entries.source: HUDM 5001 advanced track, “Building a miniGPT from an empty folder” (build guide), “Changes to the original plan”

entries.title: Step 1 · Make the project folder
entries.summary: One folder holds everything: code, tests, configuration and the (ignored) data. Create it somewhere you can find again and move into it; every command in this workflow is typed from inside this folder.
entries.example:
mkdir minigpt
cd minigpt
pwd
lines: mkdir minigpt
Makes a new, empty folder named `minigpt` inside the folder you are in (here the home folder).
cd minigpt
Moves into it. The prompt does not always show it, so the next line checks.
pwd
Prints the working directory: the full path of the folder you are in.
entries.gotcha: Short, lowercase, no spaces or hyphens: `minigpt`, not `My GPT Project`. The folder name becomes the package name in step 7, and Python cannot import a name with a space or a dash.
entries.source: HUDM 5001 advanced track, “Building a miniGPT from an empty folder” (build guide), step 1

entries.title: Step 2 · Create an isolated conda environment
entries.summary: An environment is a private Python installation that belongs to this project only. Create it with conda, turn it on with `conda activate`, then install the project's packages with pip. From now on everything you install lands here and nowhere else, and “somewhere else” is never your system Python.
entries.example:
conda create --name minigpt python=3.12 -y
conda activate minigpt
python -m pip install torch numpy pandas pyyaml matplotlib
entries.output_note: conda lists what it will install and continues without asking because of `-y`. When activation works, your prompt starts with `(minigpt)` instead of `(base)`. That prefix is the single most useful signal in the whole project: if it says `(base)`, you are about to install into your Anaconda installation instead of your project.
lines: conda create --name minigpt python=3.12 -y

Makes a new environment called `minigpt` with its own Python 3.12. `--name` gives it a name, `python=3.12` pins the version (the course default, and a version every package supports), `-y` answers “yes” to the confirmation question.
conda activate minigpt
Turns the environment on for this terminal window. Do it every time you open a new terminal to work on the project; the `(minigpt)` prefix tells you it worked.
python -m pip install torch numpy pandas pyyaml matplotlib

Installs the packages into the active environment: PyTorch for the model, NumPy and pandas for arrays and tables, PyYAML to read the config files, matplotlib for plots. `python -m pip` (rather than a bare `pip`) runs the pip that belongs to this `python`: a bare `pip` is whichever pip is first on the PATH, which on a computer with Anaconda plus a system Python is not always the same one, and then packages land where `import` cannot find them.
entries.gotcha: Use conda to create the environment and choose the Python version; use `python -m pip` for everything inside it, and do not run `conda install` afterwards: conda does not know what pip installed and can overwrite it, and the environment fails later on an import with an error that points nowhere. If an environment breaks, do not repair it: `conda deactivate`, `conda env remove --name minigpt -y`, and create it again in thirty seconds. Nothing of value lives inside one; your code is in Git and your data is regenerable.
entries.source: HUDM 5001 advanced track, “Building a miniGPT from an empty folder” (build guide), step 1

entries.title: Step 3 · Check that the right Python is active
entries.summary: Before writing anything, prove that the terminal is using the environment you just made. Four commands answer four questions: which version, which `python` file, which pip goes with it, and do the packages import.
entries.example:
python -V
which python
python -m pip --version
python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.backends.mps.is_available())"
entries.output_note: Recorded on an Apple-silicon Mac, so the GPU check prints `True`. On Windows or Linux without an NVIDIA card it prints `False`, and on Colab the check that prints `True` is `torch.cuda.is_available()`. All of these are fine: step 13 picks the device automatically.
lines: python -V
Prints the version. It must say 3.12, the version you pinned in step 2.
which python
Prints the path of the `python` command this terminal runs. The path must contain `envs/minigpt`; if it says `base` or `/usr/bin`, the environment is not active. On Windows use `where python`.
python -m pip --version

Runs pip as a module of that same `python` and prints where it lives. The path must also contain `envs/minigpt`: this is the pip that step 2 installed into, and the one every `python -m pip install` will use.
python -c "import torch; print(...)"
`-c` runs the quoted code without a file. Importing torch proves the install worked; the second value says whether the Apple GPU (MPS) can be used.
entries.gotcha: If a package imports in the terminal but not in VS Code, VS Code is using a different Python: open the Command Palette, run “Python: Select Interpreter” and choose `minigpt`, then restart the kernel.
entries.source: HUDM 5001 advanced track, “Building a miniGPT from an empty folder” (build guide), step 1 checkpoint

entries.title: Step 4 · git init, ignore first, commit second
entries.summary: Turn the folder into a Git repository, write the ignore rules and a README, and make the first commit. The order matters: Git history is append-only in practice, so anything large or private must be ignored before it is ever staged.

files.content:

.venv/
__pycache__/
*.egg-info/

# data and artefacts: regenerable from the code, so never committed
data/
checkpoints/
runs/
*.pt
*.npy

# notebook checkpoints and operating-system noise

.DS_Store

# miniGPT

A character-level language model built from an empty folder, following the
HUDM 5001 standard workflow: environment first, Git second, tests alongside.

entries.example:
git init
git add .gitignore README.md
git commit -m "Initialise repository with ignore rules"
git status
lines: .gitignore: .venv/  __pycache__/  *.egg-info/
Folders Python and pip create while you work. They are regenerated every time and belong to your machine, not to the project.
.gitignore: data/  checkpoints/  runs/  *.pt  *.npy

Everything regenerable from code: the downloaded corpus, cached arrays, trained weights, training logs. A collaborator should rebuild them by running your scripts, not download them from your repository. Rule of thumb: commit the recipe, never the result.
.gitignore: .ipynb_checkpoints/  .DS_Store
Notebook autosaves and macOS folder metadata: pure noise in a diff.
README.md
One paragraph for now: what the project is. Step 22 turns it into a real README with reproduce instructions and results.
git init
Creates the hidden `.git` folder that will store every snapshot. Run once per project.
git add .gitignore README.md
Stages exactly these two files. Naming them instead of `git add .` is a habit that keeps surprises out of the first commit.
git commit -m "Initialise repository with ignore rules"
Saves the snapshot with a message. The output names the branch, the new commit id, and the files it contains.
git status
“nothing to commit, working tree clean” means every tracked file is saved. You will see this line a lot.
entries.gotcha: Write ignore rules for things that do not exist yet (`runs/`, `*.pt`). The point is that they never get the chance to be staged.

entries.title: Step 5 · Create an empty repository on GitHub
entries.summary: GitHub is where the project lives outside your laptop: backup, sharing, and later Colab. Create the repository completely empty, so the history starts on your computer and GitHub simply receives it. Two ways to do it, same result: click through the website (A), or one command with the GitHub CLI (B). Either way, step 6 is next.
entries.example:
A · In the browser
github.com → "+" (top right) → New repository
  Repository name:  minigpt           ← the same name as your folder
  Visibility:       Public or Private
  Leave UNTICKED:   Add a README, Add .gitignore, Choose a license
→ Create repository

B · In the terminal, with the GitHub CLI
conda install -c conda-forge gh        # one time (a Mac can also use: brew install gh)
gh auth login                          # one time per computer: GitHub.com → HTTPS → Login with a web browser
gh repo create minigpt --private       # or --public
gh repo view minigpt --web             # optional: open the new page to check
entries.output_note: Route A ends on a page with a box titled “…or push an existing repository from the command line”; its three commands are step 6. Route B prints the address of the new repository, `https://github.com/<your-username>/minigpt`. Neither is recorded here because both need your GitHub account.
lines: A · Repository name
Use the folder name so the URL and the folder match: `github.com/<your-username>/minigpt`.
A · Leave the three boxes unticked
You already have a README and a .gitignore from step 4. Ticking a box makes GitHub create a first commit that your computer does not have, and your first push is rejected.
A · Create repository
Nothing is uploaded yet. The repository is an empty shell waiting for `git push`.
B · conda install -c conda-forge gh
Installs the GitHub CLI into the `minigpt` environment. `gh` is a separate program from `git`: git manages your history, gh talks to the GitHub website for you.
B · gh auth login

A one-time login per computer. Answer the questions (GitHub.com, HTTPS, Yes, Login with a web browser), copy the one-time code it shows, press Enter, paste the code on the GitHub page that opens. From now on `git push` never asks for a password: gh stored a token that git reuses.
B · gh repo create minigpt --private

Creates an empty repository named `minigpt` under your account. `--private` or `--public` is required in this form; with no name and no flag, `gh repo create` asks questions instead. Nothing is uploaded and no README is added, so it matches route A exactly.
B · gh repo view minigpt --web
Opens the repository page in your browser, the quickest check that it exists.
B · the one-command shortcut, for later

`gh repo create minigpt --private --source=. --remote=origin --push`, run inside the project folder, does steps 5 and 6 together: creates the repository, adds it as `origin`, and pushes. Learn the two-step version first so you know what it does.
entries.gotcha: If you did tick “Add a README” (route A) or added `--add-readme` (route B), the simplest fix is to delete the repository on GitHub (Settings → Danger zone) and create it again empty.
entries.source: HUDM 5001 advanced track, “Building a miniGPT from an empty folder” (build guide), step 2

entries.title: Step 6 · Connect the folder to GitHub and push
entries.summary: Copy the three commands GitHub printed. They tell Git the address of the remote copy, name the branch `main`, and upload the first commit while remembering the link, so that later pushes are just `git push`.
entries.example:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/minigpt.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
entries.output_note: Replace `YOUR-USERNAME` with your GitHub user name. On your machine the output names your GitHub URL; in this recorded run a local folder stands in for GitHub, so the output names that folder instead.
lines: git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/minigpt.git
`origin` is the conventional nickname for your GitHub copy. The URL is the one on the empty-repository page (or the green **Code** button, HTTPS tab).
git branch -M main
Renames the current branch to `main`; older Git versions start on `master`. `-M` renames even if `main` already exists.
git push -u origin main
Uploads your commits. `-u` records that local `main` follows `origin/main`, so plain `git push` and `git pull` work from now on. The output ends with the branch tracking line.
If you used the gh shortcut in step 5
`gh repo create … --source=. --remote=origin --push` already did all three lines; run `git remote -v` and you will see `origin` pointing at GitHub. Skip to step 7.
entries.gotcha: GitHub does not accept your account password over HTTPS. When asked for a password, paste a personal access token, or sign in once through GitHub Desktop or the `gh` command-line tool.

entries.title: Step 7 · Scaffold the package and install it in editable mode
entries.summary: Create the folder layout the project will grow into, describe the package in `pyproject.toml`, and install it with `pip install -e .` so that `import minigpt` works from anywhere on your machine and always points at your source folder. Make all the folders now, even the empty ones: an empty `tests/` that is waiting for you is worth more than a perfect one you meant to create later.

files.content:
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "minigpt"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.13"
dependencies = ["torch", "numpy", "pandas", "pyyaml", "matplotlib"]

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]

entries.example:
mkdir -p src/minigpt tests configs scripts notebooks data checkpoints
touch src/minigpt/__init__.py
python -m pip install -q -e .
python -m pip show minigpt
cd ..
python -c "import minigpt; print(minigpt.__file__)"
cd minigpt
git add pyproject.toml src
git commit -m "Scaffold the package"
lines: mkdir -p src/minigpt tests configs scripts notebooks data checkpoints

Seven folders at once; `-p` creates parents and does not complain if one exists. `src/minigpt/` is the importable package where all real code lives; `tests/` mirrors it; `configs/` holds YAML settings; `scripts/` one-off jobs; `notebooks/` thin demos; `data/` and `checkpoints/` are ignored by Git.
touch src/minigpt/__init__.py
Creates an empty file. Its presence tells Python that `src/minigpt` is a package.
pyproject.toml: [build-system]
Which tool builds the package (setuptools). Boilerplate you copy between projects.
pyproject.toml: [project]
Name, version, the Python range it supports, and the packages it depends on. pip reads this list.
pyproject.toml: [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"]
Tells setuptools that packages live under `src/`. This “src layout” makes it impossible to import a half-written package from the current folder by accident.
python -m pip install -q -e .

Installs the package from the current folder (`.`) in editable mode (`-e`): Python records a link to `src/`, so every edit is live with no reinstall. `python -m pip` guarantees it is this environment's pip (step 3 checked that); `-q` hides the long list of `Requirement already satisfied` lines, the packages from step 2.
python -m pip show minigpt
Proves the install: the version from `pyproject.toml`, `Editable project location` pointing at your folder, and `Requires` listing the dependencies.
cd .. / python -c "import minigpt; print(minigpt.__file__)" / cd minigpt
The test that matters: import from a folder that is *not* the project. The printed path must end in `src/minigpt/__init__.py`. Then go back into the project.
git add pyproject.toml src / git commit
Commits the scaffold. The `src/minigpt.egg-info/` folder that the install created is ignored by the `*.egg-info/` rule.
entries.gotcha: `ImportError: minigpt` later on has two usual causes: the environment is not activated (the prompt says `(base)`), or `python -m pip install -e .` was never run in this environment. A bare `pip install -e .` that used another Python's pip is the sneaky third cause; `python -m pip show minigpt` settles it.

entries.title: Step 8 · Fetch the data with a script, not by hand
entries.summary: Downloading a file by hand is fine exactly once and then becomes the thing nobody can reproduce. A twenty-line script downloads the corpus, checks its size and fingerprint, and is safe to run again. The corpus is tinyshakespeare: 1.1 MB of plays, one character at a time.

files.content:
"""Download tinyshakespeare into data/. Safe to re-run."""
import hashlib
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

URL = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/"
       "master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt")
DEST = Path("data/input.txt")
EXPECTED_BYTES = 1_115_394

def main() -> None:
    DEST.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    if not DEST.exists():
        print(f"downloading -> {DEST}")
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL, DEST)
    raw = DEST.read_bytes()
    digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()[:12]
    print(f"{len(raw):,} bytes  sha256:{digest}")
    if len(raw) != EXPECTED_BYTES:
        raise SystemExit("unexpected file size - the source may have changed")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

entries.example:
python scripts/get_data.py
python scripts/get_data.py
git status --short
git add scripts/get_data.py
git commit -m "Add the data download script"
lines: import hashlib, urllib.request, from pathlib import Path
Standard library only: hashing, downloading, and paths. Nothing to install.
URL, DEST, EXPECTED_BYTES
Three constants at the top: where the file comes from, where it goes, how big it must be. For another dataset you change these, not the code.
DEST.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Creates `data/` if needed and does not fail if it already exists.
if not DEST.exists(): ... urlretrieve(URL, DEST)
Downloads only when the file is missing, so the second run costs nothing.
digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()[:12]
A fingerprint of the bytes. If it changes later, the data changed, not your code; three lines that settle arguments.
if len(raw) != EXPECTED_BYTES: raise SystemExit(...)
Stops with a message instead of continuing with a wrong file.
if __name__ == "__main__": main()
Runs `main()` only when the file is executed as a script, not when it is imported.
python scripts/get_data.py  (twice)
The first run downloads and reports; the second only reports: same size, same fingerprint.
git status --short
Shows `?? scripts/` (untracked, new) and nothing about `data/`: the ignore rule from step 4 is doing its job.
entries.gotcha: If `git status` lists `data/input.txt`, your `.gitignore` is missing the `data/` line or has a typo. Fix it before you commit.

entries.title: Step 9 · Clean the text, and write the test in the same sitting
entries.summary: Cleaning is a list of explicit decisions about what you will and will not model, written as code so you can still see them in six weeks: normalise Unicode, flatten curly quotes, unify line endings, collapse repeated spaces and blank lines. The test checks a property (cleaning twice changes nothing) rather than one exact output.

files.content:
"""Corpus cleaning: normalise whitespace and drop characters we will not model."""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import unicodedata
from collections import Counter

SMART = {"‘": "'", "’": "'", "“": '"', "”": '"',
         "–": "-", "—": "--", "…": "..."}

def clean_text(raw: str, min_char_count: int = 0) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", raw)
    for bad, good in SMART.items():
        text = text.replace(bad, good)
    text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")
    text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text)      # runs of spaces -> one
    text = re.sub(r" *\n", "\n", text)       # trailing spaces on a line
    text = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text)   # at most one blank line
    text = text.strip() + "\n"

    if min_char_count > 0:
        counts = Counter(text)
        rare = {ch for ch, n in counts.items() if n < min_char_count}
        text = "".join(ch for ch in text if ch not in rare)
    return text

def describe(text: str) -> dict:
    counts = Counter(text)
    return {"n_chars": len(text),
            "n_lines": text.count("\n") + 1,
            "vocab_size": len(counts),
            "most_common": counts.most_common(5)}

"""Print what cleaning did to the corpus: size, vocabulary, and the most common characters."""
from pathlib import Path

from minigpt.clean import clean_text, describe

raw = Path("data/input.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
text = clean_text(raw)
r, c = describe(raw), describe(text)
print(f"raw:    {r['n_chars']:,} chars   vocab {r['vocab_size']}")
print(f"clean:  {c['n_chars']:,} chars   vocab {c['vocab_size']}   lines {c['n_lines']:,}")
print("most common:", " | ".join(f"{ch!r} {n:,}" for ch, n in c["most_common"]))

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
git add src tests scripts
git commit -m "Add the corpus cleaner and its tests"

Turns look-alike characters into one standard form (full-width letters, odd spaces), so the model does not learn two spellings of the same thing.
for bad, good in SMART.items(): text = text.replace(bad, good)
Replaces curly quotes and long dashes with their plain keyboard versions, one pair at a time.

text.replace("
", "
").replace("", "
")
Windows and old-Mac line endings become plain `\n`.
re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text)
A regular expression: one or more spaces or tabs become a single space.

re.sub(r"
{3,}", "

", text)
Three or more line breaks in a row become two: at most one blank line.

test_cleaning_twice_changes_nothing
The most valuable cleaner test: `clean(clean(x)) == clean(x)`. If cleaning twice differs from cleaning once, two of your rules are fighting.

Prints the before-and-after numbers. Only twenty characters were removed and the vocabulary stayed at 65: correct for a corpus that was already tidy.
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

entries.gotcha: Test the property, not the output. A test that pins the exact cleaned text of a whole file breaks the moment you improve one rule, and tells you nothing when it does.

entries.title: Step 10 · Write the tokenizer: a class with a round-trip test
entries.summary: A tokenizer maps text to integers and back. For a character-level model it is genuinely this small, and writing it yourself removes most of the mystery from the word “tokenization”. Five tests, and the round trip is the one that really matters.
entries.example:
python -c "from minigpt.tokenizer import CharTokenizer; tok = CharTokenizer.from_text('hello'); print(tok.chars, tok.encode('hello'), tok.decode([1, 2]))"
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
git add src tests
git commit -m "Add the character tokenizer and its tests"
lines: class CharTokenizer: def __init__(self, chars)
The vocabulary is a list of characters. `stoi` (string to int) and `itos` (int to string) are two dictionaries built from it; a duplicate character is refused with a clear error.
@classmethod def from_text(cls, text)
A second way to build one, from the text itself: `sorted(set(text))` is every distinct character in a fixed order.
@property def vocab_size(self)
A method you read like an attribute: `tok.vocab_size`, no parentheses.
encode / decode
Lists of integers from text and back. `encode` turns a missing character into a clear `ValueError` instead of a `KeyError` deep inside a loop.
save / load

entries.title: Step 11 · Split the data and produce training batches
entries.summary: Two jobs: hold out a validation slice you never train on, and turn the integer array into batches of (context, next character) pairs. The second is where most beginners write their first off-by-one bug, so a small script prints one pair for you to read.

files.content:
from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch

from minigpt.clean import clean_text
from minigpt.tokenizer import CharTokenizer

def build_arrays(src="data/input.txt", out_dir="data", val_frac=0.1):
    """Clean, tokenize, split, and cache to .npy. Returns the tokenizer."""
    out = Path(out_dir)
    text = clean_text(Path(src).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    tok = CharTokenizer.from_text(text)
    ids = np.array(tok.encode(text), dtype=np.uint16)

    n = int(len(ids) * (1 - val_frac))
    np.save(out / "train.npy", ids[:n])
    np.save(out / "val.npy", ids[n:])
    tok.save(out / "vocab.json")
    print(f"vocab {tok.vocab_size} | train {n:,} | val {len(ids) - n:,}")
    return tok

def get_batch(split_array, block_size, batch_size, device, generator=None):
    """One batch of contexts x and their next-character targets y."""
    ix = torch.randint(len(split_array) - block_size - 1,
                       (batch_size,), generator=generator)
    data = torch.from_numpy(split_array.astype(np.int64))
    x = torch.stack([data[i:i + block_size] for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([data[i + 1:i + block_size + 1] for i in ix])
    return x.to(device), y.to(device)

import torch

tok = CharTokenizer.load("data/vocab.json")
train = np.load("data/train.npy")
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
x, y = get_batch(train, block_size=8, batch_size=1, device="cpu", generator=g)

print("y:", repr(tok.decode(y[0])))

entries.title: Step 12 · Build the dumbest model first: a counting baseline
entries.summary: Before any neural network, count how often each character follows each other character, normalise the rows into probabilities, and score the validation text. No PyTorch, no gradients, under a second, and it gives you a number the transformer has to beat.

files.content:
import math
import unittest

import numpy as np

from minigpt.baseline import CountBigram


class BaselineTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_untrained_model_is_uniform(self):
        model = CountBigram(vocab_size=5)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(model.nll([0, 1, 2, 3]), math.log(5), places=6)

    def test_rows_are_probability_distributions(self):
        model = CountBigram(vocab_size=4).fit([0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 0])
        np.testing.assert_allclose(model.probs.sum(axis=1), 1.0)

    def test_fitting_lowers_the_loss(self):
        ids = [0, 1] * 50
        model = CountBigram(vocab_size=2)
        before = model.nll(ids)
        after = model.fit(ids).nll(ids)
        self.assertLess(after, before)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

entries.title: Step 14 · The transformer in four classes, with the two tests that catch almost everything
entries.summary: Build it in order and run the tests after each class. A `Head` is one attention mechanism; `MultiHeadAttention` runs several in parallel; a `Block` wraps attention plus a small feed-forward network in residual connections; `GPT` stacks blocks between an embedding table and an output layer. Two tests matter most: the loss at initialisation equals ln(65), and information does not flow backwards in time.

import math
import unittest

import torch

from minigpt.config import Config
from minigpt.model import GPT


def tiny():
    return Config(vocab_size=65, block_size=8, n_layer=2,
                  n_head=2, n_embd=32, dropout=0.0, device="cpu")


class ModelTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_output_shape(self):
        cfg = tiny()
        logits, _ = GPT(cfg)(torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (4, 8)))
        self.assertEqual(tuple(logits.shape), (4, 8, cfg.vocab_size))

    def test_loss_at_init_is_uniform(self):
        cfg = tiny()
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        x = torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (16, 8))
        y = torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (16, 8))
        _, loss = GPT(cfg)(x, y)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(loss.item(), math.log(cfg.vocab_size), delta=0.15)

    def test_attention_is_causal(self):
        cfg = tiny()
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = GPT(cfg).eval()
        a = torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (1, 8))
        b = a.clone()
        b[0, -1] = (b[0, -1] + 1) % cfg.vocab_size          # edit the future only
        with torch.no_grad():
            self.assertTrue(torch.equal(model(a)[0][:, :-1], model(b)[0][:, :-1]))

    def test_generate_respects_block_size(self):
        cfg = tiny()
        model = GPT(cfg).eval()
        out = model.generate(torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.long), 30)
        self.assertEqual(tuple(out.shape), (1, 31))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

entries.title: Step 15 · Train the walking skeleton, and log every run
entries.summary: The training loop is short; what makes it professional is everything around it: a fixed seed, a loss averaged over many batches instead of one noisy one, a CSV you can plot, a `manifest.json` recording which commit produced which number, and a checkpoint of the best validation loss. Always run the tiny config first: seconds, and it tells you whether the whole pipeline is wired correctly.

files.content:
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import json
import subprocess
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch

from minigpt.config import Config
from minigpt.data import get_batch
from minigpt.model import GPT

def git_commit() -> str:
    try:
        out = subprocess.run(["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"],
                             capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        return out.stdout.strip()
    except Exception:
        return "unknown"

@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss(model, splits, cfg):
    """Average loss over many batches - one batch is far too noisy to steer by."""
    model.eval()
    out = {}
    for name, arr in splits.items():
        losses = torch.zeros(cfg.eval_iters)
        for k in range(cfg.eval_iters):
            x, y = get_batch(arr, cfg.block_size, cfg.batch_size, cfg.device)
            losses[k] = model(x, y)[1].item()
        out[name] = losses.mean().item()
    model.train()
    return out

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--config", default="configs/base.yaml")
    ap.add_argument("--run-name", default=None)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    cfg = Config.from_yaml(args.config)
    torch.manual_seed(cfg.seed)
    np.random.seed(cfg.seed)

    run = args.run_name or time.strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
    run_dir = Path("runs") / run
    run_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    splits = {"train": np.load("data/train.npy"),
              "val": np.load("data/val.npy")}
    model = GPT(cfg).to(cfg.device)
    print(f"{model.n_params() / 1e6:.2f}M parameters on {cfg.device}")

    # the manifest ties every number you report to the exact code that made it
    (run_dir / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(
        {"config": cfg.to_dict(), "commit": git_commit(),
         "params": model.n_params(), "started": run}, indent=2))

    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=cfg.learning_rate)
    log = open(run_dir / "log.csv", "w", newline="")
    writer = csv.writer(log)
    writer.writerow(["iter", "train_loss", "val_loss", "seconds"])

    best, t0 = float("inf"), time.time()
    for it in range(cfg.max_iters + 1):
        if it % cfg.eval_interval == 0 or it == cfg.max_iters:
            losses = estimate_loss(model, splits, cfg)
            dt = time.time() - t0
            print(f"iter {it:5d} | train {losses['train']:.4f} "
                  f"| val {losses['val']:.4f} | {dt:6.1f}s")
            writer.writerow([it, losses["train"], losses["val"], round(dt, 1)])
            log.flush()
            if losses["val"] < best:
                best = losses["val"]
                torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(),
                            "config": cfg.to_dict(), "iter": it, "val_loss": best},
                           run_dir / "best.pt")

        x, y = get_batch(splits["train"], cfg.block_size, cfg.batch_size, cfg.device)
        loss = model(x, y)[1]
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        opt.step()

    log.close()
    print(f"best validation loss {best:.4f} -> {run_dir / 'best.pt'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

import torch

from minigpt.config import Config
from minigpt.model import GPT
from minigpt.tokenizer import CharTokenizer

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--checkpoint", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=500)
    ap.add_argument("--temperature", type=float, default=0.8)
    ap.add_argument("--top-k", type=int, default=None)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=None)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    if args.seed is not None:
        torch.manual_seed(args.seed)

    ck = torch.load(args.checkpoint, map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
    cfg = Config(**ck["config"])
    tok = CharTokenizer.load("data/vocab.json")

    model = GPT(cfg)
    model.load_state_dict(ck["model"])
    model.to(cfg.device).eval()

    start = torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.long, device=cfg.device)
    out = model.generate(start, args.n, args.temperature, args.top_k)
    print(tok.decode(out[0].tolist()))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Plot train and validation loss from a run's log.csv, with the two reference lines."""
import sys

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

run = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "runs/base"
df = pd.read_csv(f"{run}/log.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(df["iter"], df["train_loss"], label="train")
ax.plot(df["iter"], df["val_loss"], label="validation")
ax.axhline(2.4819, ls="--", lw=1, color="gray", label="counting bigram")
ax.axhline(4.1744, ls=":", lw=1, color="gray", label="untrained")
ax.set(xlabel="iteration", ylabel="cross-entropy (nats)")
ax.legend()

fig.savefig(f"{run}/curve.png", dpi=110)

entries.title: Step 18 · Consolidate the test suite: one command, seconds, no data
entries.summary: By now every module has its tests. Add the one that covers the seams: overfit a single batch on purpose. If the model cannot memorise four sequences it sees two hundred times, the training wiring is broken, and you find out in three seconds instead of after an hour of training. The whole suite must run in seconds without touching `data/` or the network.

files.content:
import unittest

import torch

from minigpt.config import Config
from minigpt.model import GPT


class TrainingTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_model_can_overfit_one_batch(self):
        """If it cannot memorise 4 sequences, the training wiring is broken."""
        cfg = Config(vocab_size=65, block_size=8, n_layer=2, n_head=2,
                     n_embd=32, dropout=0.0, device="cpu")
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        model = GPT(cfg)
        x = torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (4, 8))
        y = torch.randint(0, cfg.vocab_size, (4, 8))

        opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
        first = model(x, y)[1].item()
        for _ in range(200):
            loss = model(x, y)[1]
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
        self.assertLess(loss.item(), first / 4)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

    python scripts/get_data.py && python -c "from minigpt.data import build_arrays; build_arrays()"

## Results

| model               | val loss | perplexity |
|---------------------|----------|------------|
| uniform (untrained) |  4.174   |   65.0     |
| counting bigram     |  2.482   |   12.0     |
| miniGPT 10.8M       |  1.466   |   4.3     |
